title: The Hollowing of the Venezuelan State
text:
Introduction by Sophia Grace Carter 

 I n September , the photojournalist Lynsey Addario traveled to Venezuela with Atlantic staff writer Anne Applebaum. They arrived in a country devastated by back-to-back earthquakes in June and still reeling from the U.S. military operation that had toppled its president, Nicolás Maduro, in January. Drawing on her reporting there, Applebaum argues in The Atlantic ’s December issue that the Trump administration has revived a familiar form of Yankee imperialism, laying claim to Venezuela’s oil troves with little regard for the interests of its people. Addario’s images capture the head-spinning transformations under way—and how some citizens are chafing against the new political order and others are attempting to preserve some semblance of normalcy.

 [ From the December 2026 issue: Anne Applebaum on what the U.S. is really doing in Venezuela ] 

 Addario has covered nearly every major global conflict of the past two decades—the U.S. invasions of Afghanistan and Iraq, the genocide in Darfur, the civil wars in Libya and Syria, Russia’s incursion into Ukraine. But she began her career in Latin America at 21, traveling through the region with her camera. In 2002, she documented the aftermath of a failed coup attempt against the regime of Hugo Chávez, Maduro’s predecessor, and, in 2024, for this magazine, she photographed a group of migrants crossing the Darién Gap , many of them Venezuelan. Nearly 8 million Venezuelans—about 25 percent of the population —have fled the country over the past decade. 

 On this year’s trip, she witnessed the circumstances that have driven that exodus. Once the richest country in South America, Venezuela now suffers from the world’s highest inflation rate, driven by a quarter century of political fracturing, corruption, economic mismanagement, and U.S. sanctions. Though the country possesses the world’s largest proven oil reserves—more than 300 billion barrels—electricity shortages are a fact of life, and many Venezuelans live in poverty amid crumbling infrastructure. 

 When the earthquakes struck in June, the government’s ineffectual response left citizens to fend for themselves. The tremors killed at least 6,500 people; injured more than 16,800; and left about 17,000 homeless. In La Guaira, the city hardest hit, government rescue workers didn’t show up for days, so residents and volunteers mobilized to deliver aid on their own, turning schools into makeshift shelters and opening soup kitchens.

 Heeding the war photographer Robert Capa’s dictum that “If your pictures aren’t good enough, you’re not close enough,” Addario often spends time talking with her subjects before photographing them, trying to understand their life and circumstances. These conversations can be fraught, and Addario told me that she sometimes becomes the target of her subjects’ anger and frustration. But she can also serve as an outlet for them. In La Guaira, where she encountered people digging through the wreckage with their bare hands in search of the bodies of the missing, she sensed that some were grateful to have their loss memorialized. Months had passed, and they were still there searching. By photographing them, Addario hoped she might help ensure that “they don’t feel like it’s all been forgotten.”

 — Sophia Grace Carter 

 Lynsey Addario for The Atlantic 

 Jeanpier Bolívar, 34, and Juan José Meléndez, 27, pull in a nearly empty fishing net on Lake Maracaibo, a brackish estuary where oil extraction began more than a century ago. The lake is South America’s largest body of water—and its largest environmental disaster. Local fishermen say their catches have dwindled as pollution has worsened, and some resort to rinsing their crabs and shrimp with gasoline to remove the crude oil. 

 Lynsey Addario for The Atlantic 

 A thick sheen of petroleum coats the lake’s surface. More than two decades of neglect have left its waters poisoned by leaks and spills, and dotted with ghostly drilling platforms.

 Lynsey Addario for The Atlantic 

 The oil industry has generated enormous wealth, even as many of the people living in the shadow of its pumps and refineries remain mired in poverty. 

 Lynsey Addario for The Atlantic 

 Residents gather on a street in the city of Maracaibo during a rolling blackout. Though Venezuela has the world’s largest proven oil reserves, the country’s deteriorating electrical grid causes regular power outages lasting six to eight hours.

 Lynsey Addario for The Atlantic 

 A street market in Maracaibo in September. Skyrocketing inflation has driven up the cost of basic goods; prices sometimes change from one day to the next.

 Lynsey Addario for The Atlantic 

 Venezuelans ride on public transportation in La Vega. The neighborhood was once a stronghold of Hugo Chávez, who ruled Venezuela from 1999 until his death in 2013. 

 Lynsey Addario for The Atlantic 

 A boy plays in an alley in La Vega. 

 Lynsey Addario for The Atlantic 

 Venezuelans were still searching for the bodies of loved ones amid mountains of brick and concrete in La Guaira in September, more than two months after back-to-back earthquakes devastated the region.

 Lynsey Addario for The Atlantic 

 Women pray during an open-air Mass at the Basílica de Santa Teresa in Caracas. The church was damaged by the June earthquakes and declared unsafe to enter. 

 Lynsey Addario for The Atlantic 

 Venezuelan security forces barricade streets leading to Miraflores, the presidential palace in Caracas, as protesters demand the release of political prisoners. More than 320 remained incarcerated as of late October.

 Lynsey Addario for The Atlantic 

 A woman dressed as the Statue of Liberty bound in chains faces a line of Venezuelan security forces during a demonstration in Caracas.

 Lynsey Addario for The Atlantic 

 Anti-American graffiti in Caracas evokes decades of tension between Venezuela and the United States, even as Washington exerts growing influence over the country’s pliant interim government.
